young.html: F. Scott Fitzgerald was an American writer of the 1920s, the "Jazz Age," when many people in New York got rich quickly, danced to new music and threw big parties.

In The Great Gatsby, a young man named Nick moves into a little house on Long Island, next door to a huge mansion. Its owner, the mysterious Jay Gatsby, throws enormous parties every weekend. Nick learns that Gatsby once loved a young woman named Daisy, who lives across the bay. Every night Gatsby looks across the water at a green light at the end of her dock. He has made himself rich hoping to win her back, as if he could bring back the past. It doesn't end happily.

young.html: For parents: the novel includes drinking, an unfaithful marriage, a fatal car accident and a shooting, all told without graphic detail. It is usually read in high school.

Your green light. Gatsby's green light stood for a dream he reached toward. Draw a picture of a light far away across water, and inside it draw or write a dream of yours. Then talk about it: what is a good dream to work toward? Can a dream ever be the wrong one?

full.html: F. Scott Fitzgerald (1896–1940) was born in St. Paul, Minnesota, went to Princeton, and served in the army in 1917–19, though he was never sent overseas. His first novel, This Side of Paradise (1920), made him famous, and he and his wife Zelda became symbols of the high-living twenties. The Great Gatsby (1925) sold modestly in his lifetime; it was only after his early death that it came to be seen as one of the great American novels.
The narrator, Nick Carraway, begins with a lesson from his father:

full.text:
In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I've been turning over in my mind ever since.

“Whenever you feel like criticizing anyone,” he told me, “just remember that all the people in this world haven't had the advantages that you've had.”
full.author: Fitzgerald

full.html: In the summer of 1922 Nick rents a cottage in West Egg, Long Island, beside the mansion of Jay Gatsby. Across the bay, in fashionable East Egg, live Nick's cousin Daisy and her rich, arrogant husband, Tom Buchanan. On his first night Nick sees his neighbor alone on the lawn:

full.text: …he stretched out his arms toward the dark water in a curious way, and, far as I was from him, I could have sworn he was trembling. Involuntarily I glanced seaward—and distinguished nothing except a single green light, minute and far away, that might have been the end of a dock.
full.author: Fitzgerald

full.html: Gatsby, we learn, was born James Gatz to poor farm people in North Dakota. As a young officer in 1917 he fell in love with Daisy, but he had no money, and while he was away at war she married Tom. Gatsby has since made a fortune by shady means, bought a mansion across from hers, and thrown parties in the hope she might wander in. Nick arranges a reunion. For a while Gatsby believes he can have Daisy back and erase the five years between. In a hot afternoon's quarrel at the Plaza Hotel in New York, Tom exposes Gatsby, and Daisy draws back. On the drive home, Gatsby's car, with Daisy at the wheel, strikes and kills a woman. Gatsby takes the blame, and the woman's grieving husband later shoots him. Almost no one comes to his funeral. Disgusted with the careless rich, Nick goes home to the Midwest.

full.html: Gatsby's dream is part love and part the American hope of remaking oneself. Fitzgerald honors the hope and shows its corruption: money cannot buy back the past, and the people with the most money are often the most careless.
Nick is a witness who is also part of the story. He says he is honest and slow to judge, yet he helps arrange the reunion and keeps others' secrets. Reading closely means asking how far to trust him.
Treating the novel as a celebration of parties and wealth. The glamour is real, but the book is closer to a lament: the parties are empty, and their host dies alone.

items: Cather's A Lost Lady, two years earlier and on this ladder, also shows a young man watching a glamorous figure and an age passing.
Conrad's Heart of Darkness uses a witness-narrator, Marlow, telling of a mysterious man; Fitzgerald admired Conrad and learned from him.
Veblen's Theory of the Leisure Class, in this era's social science, named the "conspicuous consumption" that Gatsby's parties put on show.
Franklin's Autobiography lies behind the young Gatsby's schedule of self-improvement, which his father shows Nick after the funeral.
Can a person remake himself completely? What would be lost?
Why does Gatsby believe he can repeat the past?
Who in the novel is careless, and what does carelessness cost others?

questions: Nick's father told him not to judge others too quickly. Is that good advice?
What did the green light mean to Gatsby?
Gatsby worked hard for his dream. Was it a good dream?
Why do you think so few people came to Gatsby's funeral?
Can money make a person happy? What does this story say?
